questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: How the molecular speed scales with temperature
questions.learningObjective: Identify how the molecular speed scales with temperature.
questions.stem: A depot stores nitrogen in a rigid tank whose gas starts at 300 K. If the temperature rises to 600 K, how does the rms molecular speed change?

options.text: It increases by a factor of sqrt(2), so about 1.41 times the original speed.
It doubles, because the average molecular speed is directly proportional to the temperature in kelvin.
options.misconception: believes speed is directly proportional to absolute temperature

options.text: It increases by a factor of four, since the gas absorbs four times as much energy.
options.misconception: confuses quadrupled energy with quadrupled speed

options.text: It stays the same, because the number of molecules determines the average speed.
options.misconception: believes the molecule count fixes the average speed

questions.explanation: The rms speed scales as the square root of absolute temperature, so doubling T multiplies it by sqrt(2). Energy scales with T itself, so quadrupled energy means only doubled speed.
questions.hint: Compare the kinetic energy, which is linear in T, with speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Effect of adding gas at fixed volume
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of adding gas at fixed volume.
questions.stem: A rigid depot tank is filled with helium at 1.0 atm and 300 K. More helium is pumped in until the moles double while the volume stays fixed and the tank remains in thermal equilibrium with the depot. What happens to the pressure?

options.text: The pressure rises to 2.0 atm because pressure is proportional to the number of moles at fixed V and T.
The pressure stays at 1.0 atm because the tank walls hold the pressure constant at fixed volume.
options.misconception: believes a rigid container pins the pressure

options.text: The pressure rises to about 1.41 atm because the added gas shares the space more thinly.
options.misconception: confuses added moles with a temperature change

options.text: The pressure drops to 0.5 atm because each added molecule displaces an original one.
options.misconception: thinks added gas reduces the pressure per molecule

questions.explanation: At fixed volume and temperature, P = nRT/V, so doubling the moles doubles the pressure to 2.0 atm. A rigid wall fixes the volume, not the pressure, and adding gas leaves the temperature unchanged.
questions.hint: Use the ideal gas law and hold V and T fixed.

questions.stem: A depot compressor follows a path on a pressure-volume diagram: it holds 2.0 L and rises from 100 kPa to 300 kPa, then expands at 300 kPa from 2.0 L to 5.0 L. Find the work done in the constant-pressure part.

options.text: 900 J, since the work equals the constant pressure times the volume change of 3.0 L.
600 J, because the average of the two pressures is used for the whole cycle.
options.misconception: averages pressures instead of holding the constant one

options.text: 300 J, since only the final pressure multiplies the change in volume.
options.misconception: multiplies by the final pressure and drops the initial

options.text: 1000 J, since the area under the vertical segment is added to the expansion.
options.misconception: adds a zero-area vertical segment into the work

questions.explanation: Work done by the gas is the area under the path, so the constant-pressure part gives W = P dV = 300 kPa times 3.0 L = 900 J. The vertical segment encloses no area, so it contributes nothing.

questions.stem: A bus brake reclaimer removes heat from a cylinder while the gas expands slowly at constant temperature. Given that the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change, what must be true of the heat removed?

options.text: Heat must leave the gas, and its magnitude equals the work the gas does.
Heat must leave the gas, and it must be larger than the work done by the gas.
options.misconception: assumes heat flow always exceeds work done

options.text: No heat may flow, because a constant temperature forbids any energy transfer.
options.misconception: equates isothermal with zero heat transfer

options.text: Heat must enter the gas to keep the temperature constant during expansion.
options.misconception: confuses constant temperature with heating

questions.explanation: For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, so an isothermal change has dU = 0 and the first law gives Q = W. Heat leaves the gas in exactly the amount of work it performs.

questions.learningObjective: State what sets the internal energy of an ideal gas.
questions.stem: A planner argues that the internal energy of a sealed ideal gas cannot change because the tank is closed. How should this argument be judged?

options.text: Correct, because a sealed tank exchanges no matter and therefore no energy.
options.misconception: believes sealed means no energy exchange at all

options.text: Wrong, because heat and work can cross the walls of a sealed tank.
Correct, because only matter carries energy into or out of a tank.
options.misconception: believes energy cannot cross a closed wall

options.text: Wrong, because a sealed tank forces the temperature to stay constant.
options.misconception: believes sealed tanks hold a fixed temperature

questions.explanation: Sealing the tank stops matter from entering or leaving, but energy still crosses the boundary as heat and work, so the internal energy can change. For an ideal gas that change is fixed by the temperature change.
questions.hint: Distinguish sealing from thermal isolation.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Internal energy of a monatomic gas
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the internal energy of a monatomic gas.
questions.stem: A depot heater raises 0.30 mol of monatomic ideal gas from 300 K to 500 K. Find the change in internal energy in joules, using U = 1.5 n R T.
questions.explanation: The change in internal energy is 1.5 n R dT = 1.5 times 0.30 times 8.314 times 200, about 748.26 J. Only the temperature change matters, since the amount of gas stays fixed.
questions.hint: Use the temperature change in the U formula.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: How the molecular speed scales with temperature
questions.learningObjective: Identify how the molecular speed scales with temperature.
questions.stem: A chart plots rms speed of a fixed gas against temperature for two gas samples that differ only in molecular mass. Which observation matches theory?

options.text: Both curves rise linearly with a slope that depends only on the temperature axis.
options.misconception: predicts a linear and mass-independent rise

options.text: The heavier sample always shows the higher speed at every temperature.
options.misconception: claims heavier molecules move faster

options.text: The curves are straight lines with the lighter sample having the gentler slope.
options.misconception: mixes a linear law with a mass effect

options.text: Both curves rise like a square root, with the heavier sample lying lower at each T.

questions.explanation: Since v = sqrt(3kT/m), each curve rises with the square root of temperature and the heavier molecule gives the lower curve at every temperature. Neither curve is a straight line through the origin.
questions.hint: The mass of the molecule sits under the square root.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Effect of adding gas at fixed volume
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of adding gas at fixed volume.
questions.stem: A worker pumps gas into a rigid tank and reports that the pressure fell because the tank was cooling as the gas went in. What is the problem with that report?

options.text: There is no problem, because cooling always lowers the pressure of a gas.
options.misconception: believes cooling always lowers the pressure

options.text: Adding gas at fixed volume raises the pressure, so a fall needs an explanation.
The problem is that the tank must be heated for the gas to enter at all.
options.misconception: claims gas cannot enter a tank without heating

options.text: The problem is that pressure changes never happen without a change in volume.
options.misconception: believes pressure can change only with volume

questions.explanation: At fixed volume the pressure follows the mole count, so pumping gas in must raise the pressure while the tank stays at depot temperature. A reported fall needs some other explanation, such as a leak.
questions.hint: At fixed V, pressure tracks the number of moles.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Work read from a pressure-volume diagram
questions.learningObjective: Read the work from a pressure-volume diagram.
questions.stem: A depot cycle has an expansion at 250 kPa from 1.0 L to 4.0 L followed by a compression at 100 kPa back to 1.0 L. Give the net work done by the gas in joules.
questions.explanation: The expansion does 250 kPa times 3.0 L = 750 J and the compression does -100 kPa times 3.0 L = -300 J, so the net work is 450 J. This is also the area of the rectangle enclosed on the diagram.
questions.hint: Add the two legs with their signs.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Which segment of a diagram does no work
questions.learningObjective: Identify the diagram segment that does no work.
questions.stem: A planner asks which of two legs on a pressure-volume board can transfer energy as work: one is vertical and one is slanted downward to the left.

options.text: Only the slanted leg, because its volume changes while the vertical leg's does not.
Only the vertical leg, because it is the steeper segment of the path.
options.misconception: picks the steeper segment as the working one

options.text: Both legs, because they belong to the same closed loop of the cycle.
options.misconception: believes closed-loop membership creates work

options.text: Neither leg, because the loop returns to where it started.
options.misconception: believes closed loops transfer no work

questions.explanation: Work needs a change of volume, and the slanted leg changes volume while the vertical leg does not. Membership in a closed loop says nothing about work, and the loop's net work is the enclosed area.
questions.hint: Check the volume change along each leg.
